D2.why: Stop-doing item 1, also in the one-screen verdict, is 'Buying chains to match a rival's store count', followed by no second-best sites, not treating 3,000 stores as the goal, and not building the PBM as a business in its own right; nothing dismantles the drugstore core.

D3.why: Brutal fact 1 (High, and the verdict's most urgent) is payers pushing prescription margins down as the prescription share of sales rises and gross margin slips, with the consequence stated; fact 2 is the consolidating rival and fact 6 is mail order and PBMs diverting visits.

D5.why: The key's decline_risks_expected is empty and later_history records only a growth slowdown beyond the 10-year window, with no decline mechanism to grade against.

D7.why: Derived arithmetic is shown and correct, assumptions are tagged, and the missing metrics (profit per visit, same-store sales, cohort returns, shareholder returns) are flagged; but a few inferences are unmarked, such as closings continuing at about 88 a year to reach '~2,720 stores' and the rival merger being 'partly to gain payer leverage'.

D8.why: The verdict leads with the hedgehog sentence, weakest flywheel link, top three stop-doing items, most urgent brutal fact and missing numbers, and is actionable, but with the score, overall paragraph and run notes it runs somewhat past one phone screen.

D9.why: It keeps the hedgehog the company already lives by and gives subject-specific warning signs, but labels the subject 'good, with a credible path to great' (70/100, three conditional gates) and adds an eight-item stop-doing list, three new seats and metro deferrals instead of plainly saying it is already great.
